comment: The large-scale structure of the wiki: parts in reading order, and suggested paths through them. Validated by tools/check_wiki.py and used by tools/preview.py.

parts.title: The block structure
parts.subtitle: Nested blocks, congruent children, and the decimation identity they make exact.
parts.intro: Six articles establish the object everything else rests on: a group whose balls are cosets of nested finite-index subgroups, with the same number of children at every scale. The child decomposition says that every pair of vertices in different children of a block sits at the top level of that block, which is what makes the energy split into the children plus one interaction between their sums. The decimation identity is that statement written as an identity for partition functions, and it is the whole reason the renormalisation group is exact here. The fourth article passes from the blocks to the lattice, where the two-point function and the phase live; the fifth isolates what the argument actually uses and carries it to the p-adic integers; and the sixth describes the phase diagram from monotonicity alone, ending where the recursion has to take over.

parts.title: The renormalisation group
parts.subtitle: The map on block-spin laws, its fixed points, and the exponents read off them.
parts.intro: The part has one object: the rescaled decimation map on laws on the line, of which the model is an orbit. It builds the operator; solves it exactly in the Gaussian case, where the orbit closes on the variance; reads off a fixed point the two numbers that matter, the multiplier of the linearisation, which gives the correlation-length exponent, and the growth of the block spin, which the autonomy of the recursion fixes for every fixed point of this model; and turns them into the exponent dictionary by algebra. That dictionary is an if-then statement, and the article after it supplies the 'if' for the hierarchical Ising model, a nontrivial fixed point with a spectrum, which is the theorem of Bleher and Sinai. With the spectrum in hand the corrections to the power laws follow from the subleading eigenvalues; the second existence proof, Koch and Wittwer's, is valid without a small parameter; and the part closes with the flow described globally rather than near a single fixed point.

parts.title: Percolation, vectors, and the Euclidean comparison
parts.subtitle: What changes when the order parameter is a set, a vector, or a field on Z^d.
parts.intro: The same block structure carries models that are not the scalar spin model, and each one changes something specific. Percolation replaces the block-spin law by a cluster partition, and the mechanism that survives is amplification: two large clusters in sibling blocks are joined at a rate proportional to the product of their sizes. Vector spins make the block spin a vector, so the direction becomes an observable, and at criticality it does not settle. The phi-fourth truncation is where the infinite-dimensionality of the flow shows up, and the Euclidean comparison is where the exactness is lost.

paths.title: The short path
paths.note: Five articles, about an hour: the block structure, the identity, the map, the one case solved exactly, and the exponents.

paths.title: The full argument
paths.note: All fourteen, in order. Each part opens with what it adds to the one before.

paths.title: The literature first
paths.note: For a reader who wants the sources: the fixed point theorem, the vector case, the truncations, then the two rigorous analyses of the fixed point, with the reading maps alongside.

paths.title: Coming from percolation
paths.note: The model, the identity, the percolation recursion and its two exponents, then what fails on Z^d.

paths.title: Straight to the exponents
paths.note: Five articles for a reader who wants the numbers: the map, the one case solved exactly, the threshold computed from the spectrum, the dictionary, and the theorem that supplies its inputs.

paths.title: For a probabilist
paths.note: The measure-theoretic spine: the lattice as a group, its isometries, the finite-volume measures, the passage to the limit, and the phase diagram that monotonicity gives.
